common_name: Tiny Treasure Dahlia (White Miniature Pompon Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; this stocky, compact pompon type needs little staking and is well suited to tight spacing.

directions: A true miniature pompon dahlia with perfectly spherical, 1.5-inch blooms in pure white, Tiny Treasure forms a stocky, compact plant that stays tidy without heavy staking. Its small, densely packed florets are involute along their full length, the hallmark of exhibition pompon form, making it a favorite for buttonhole work and mixed bouquets. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the compact habit flowering from midsummer into fall.

common_name: Kasasagi Dahlia (Yellow-and-Red Bicolor Miniature Pompon Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; a Japanese-bred pompon type that stays a manageable height for borders and fall arrangements.

directions: Named for the Japanese word for magpie, Kasasagi produces cheerful 2-inch pompon blooms that mix yellow and red on the same flower, giving each cluster of blooms a lively, showy look that pairs especially well with autumn color schemes. The plant holds a neat, rounded habit to about 3.5 feet and produces enough stems for steady cutting through the season. Deadhead often to keep new buds coming and stake lightly in windy sites since the fully double blooms add weight to the stems.

common_name: Amber Queen Dahlia (Bronze Miniature Pompon Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; an early-flowering pompon type that starts blooming well before most other dahlias.

directions: Amber Queen is valued by cutting-garden growers for being one of the earliest pompon dahlias to flower, opening warm bronze, perfectly round 2-inch blooms well ahead of most of its class and continuing prolifically for the rest of the season. The upright 3.5-4 foot plant carries plenty of stems suited to bunching and small arrangements. Pinch the growing tip once after several sets of leaves to build a bushier plant and feed lightly through summer to sustain the heavy bloom count.

common_name: Bride to Be Dahlia (Pristine White Compact Waterlily Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; this compact waterlily type is well behaved in borders and needs only light staking.

directions: True to the waterlily form, Bride to Be opens broad, shallow 4-inch blooms of unblemished white with just a few layers of flat, slightly cupped petals, giving the flower an airy, lily-pad-like outline rather than the dense double look of ball or decorative types. The compact 3.5-foot plant stays tidy enough for containers while still supplying plenty of stems for cutting. Its clean white color and classic form make it a popular choice for bridal bouquets and other white-themed arrangements; deadhead regularly to keep fresh buds opening.

common_name: Ahoy Matey Dahlia (Mauve-Purple-to-Orange Laciniated Novelty Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; stake plants early since the heavily split petals add bulk to each bloom.

directions: Ahoy Matey is a novelty dahlia grown for its heavily laciniated petals, each one split and frayed along its length into fine filaments that give the bloom an unusually fuzzy, feathery texture rather than a smooth cactus or decorative surface. The coloring shifts across the flower from mauve-purple toward orange, an unusual combination that makes individual stems stand out in mixed arrangements. Grow it like other large-flowered garden dahlias, staking early and cutting frequently to encourage side shoots and a longer bloom season.

common_name: Giggles Dahlia (Coral-Orange Collarette Dahlia with Lavender-Pink Collar)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; the single ring of outer petals plus open center make this an excellent pollinator-friendly dahlia.

directions: Giggles pairs an unusual color combination in collarette form: a single outer ring of coral-orange ray florets surrounds an open central disc, with a smaller inner collar of soft lavender-pink petaloids sitting just inside the main petals. The contrast between the two colors gives each 3.5-inch bloom real presence in the garden despite its modest size. It is an exceptionally heavy bloomer on a 3.5-foot plant, and because the center stays open rather than fully double, it draws pollinators far more readily than ball or decorative types.

common_name: American Beauty Dahlia (Bright Orange Collarette Dahlia with Golden Collar)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; a vigorous, prolific collarette type that benefits from mid-season staking.

directions: American Beauty carries bright orange, 3.5-inch collarette blooms outlined in bright yellow, with a matching yellow inner collar that frames the open central disc. The bicolor effect is bold enough to stand out at a distance, and the 4.5-foot plant is an unusually prolific bloomer that keeps producing new flowers through the season with routine deadheading. Give it full sun and stake early, since the vigorous, upright growth habit can lean once loaded with blooms.

common_name: Citron du Cap Dahlia (Pale Yellow Laciniated Cactus Dahlia with Rose Blush)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; stake early since the large, heavily split blooms are substantial once fully open.

directions: Citron du Cap produces big, 7-inch cactus-type blooms in a delicate pale yellow, with a light dusting of rose blush over the petal tips. Heavy lacination, where each narrow petal is split and frayed along its edges, gives the flower an extremely lacy, airy texture that photographs beautifully and holds up well once cut. The 4-foot plant produces enough long stems for regular cutting, and its long vase life makes it a favorite for arrangers as well as garden display.

common_name: Bashful Dahlia (Burgundy Single Dahlia with Fuchsia Tips)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; this compact single-flowered type needs no staking and suits the front of a border.

directions: Bashful is a compact single-flowered dahlia whose 3-inch blooms combine deep burgundy petals with fuchsia tips set off by a golden-yellow center disc, a striking combination for a plant that stays under 2.5 feet tall. Because the flower has just one ring of open petals around a visible disc, it is far more attractive to bees and other pollinators than fully double types. It flowers prolifically over a long season and makes a reliable, low-maintenance bedding and cutting dahlia for the front of a border.

common_name: Linna Dahlia (Golden-Yellow Orchid-Flowering Dahlia with Rose-Tipped Petals)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; a compact orchid-flowering type that covers itself in bloom and suits containers.

directions: Linna is an orchid-flowering dahlia whose single row of narrow, slightly rolled petals opens golden yellow and blends toward rose at the tips, producing a bicolor 5-inch bloom typical of the orchid class. The compact 2.5-foot plant is so floriferous that it is largely hidden beneath its own flowers at peak bloom, making it an outstanding choice for pots and the front of a sunny border. Deadhead regularly to keep the display going and divide crowded tuber clumps every year or two for the best bloom count.

common_name: Mikayla Miranda Dahlia (White-to-Lavender-Pink Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; stake early since this short, stocky plant carries unusually large blooms for its height.

directions: Mikayla Miranda produces gorgeous 7-inch formal decorative blooms that shift from white at the base of each petal to a soft lavender-pink toward the tips, a two-tone effect that reads as a gentle blush from a distance. Unusually for a dahlia of this bloom size, the plant stays short and stocky at about 3.5 feet, giving it a full, well-filled habit rather than a tall, leggy one. Stake it early all the same, since the large flowers add considerable weight relative to the compact frame, and cut regularly for a steady supply of show-quality stems.

common_name: Bridezilla Dahlia (Pure White Giant Waterlily Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; this tall, strong-stemmed waterlily type needs sturdy staking from early in the season.

directions: Bridezilla is a larger-flowered companion to the popular Bride to Be, carrying 6-inch waterlily blooms of pure, unmarked white on broad, slightly cupped petals in the classic shallow waterlily form. Reaching about 5 feet with a strong, upright growth habit, it produces long, straight stems that are excellent for cutting and large arrangements. Because the plant grows considerably taller than most waterlily types, stake it early and firmly to keep the heavy blooms from toppling in wind and rain.

common_name: Lights Out Dahlia (Velvety Black-Red Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; its dense, hedge-like habit makes an effective dark-flowered garden backdrop.

directions: Lights Out bears 3.5-inch decorative blooms in a velvety black-red so deep it reads almost black in low light, a striking contrast against its own dark green foliage. The plant grows in a dense, almost hedge-like mass to about 3.5 feet, making it as useful as a garden backdrop or informal screen as it is a cut flower. Its abundant, evenly sized blooms hold their rich color well in full sun, and regular cutting keeps new buds coming through the season.

common_name: Boogie Nites Dahlia (Deep Purple Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; a vigorous plant that throws good lateral stems for repeat cutting.

directions: Boogie Nites produces 5-inch decorative blooms in a true, saturated deep purple, a color that holds its intensity rather than fading in strong sun. The 4.5-foot plant branches freely, sending out good lateral stems that extend the cutting season well beyond the first flush of terminal blooms. Stake it early to support the eventual flower weight, and deadhead consistently to keep the vivid purple color coming through late summer and fall.

common_name: Voodoo Dahlia (Black-Red Decorative Cut-Flower Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; lush foliage and long cutting stems make this a strong choice for cutting gardens.

directions: Voodoo carries 5-inch decorative blooms in a black-red so deep and glossy that the flowers seem to glow against lighter companions in a vase. Grown on a 4.5-foot plant with lush, full foliage, it produces excellent cutting stems and holds up well once cut, making it a favorite of cut-flower growers as much as garden dahlia collectors. Give it full sun and consistent moisture, and stake early since the mature plant carries a heavy flush of bloom.

common_name: Honeymoon Dahlia (Golden Peach-Apricot Decorative Dahlia with Lavender Blush)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; stake the upright plant early to support its full, heavy blooms.

directions: Honeymoon opens full, rounded 5-inch decorative blooms in a rich golden peach-apricot with a soft lavender blush underlying the warmer tones, a subtle color blend that shifts appearance depending on the light. The attractive 4-foot plant is a dependable bloomer across the season and pairs equally well in mixed garden beds or as a cut flower. Full sun brings out the richest color, and routine deadheading keeps new buds opening steadily into fall.

common_name: Hakuyou Dahlia (Giant White Dinnerplate Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; a late-season giant dinnerplate type, so give it the longest growing season possible and stake heavily.

directions: Hakuyou produces magnificent 12-inch pure white blooms, placing it solidly in the giant dinnerplate class even though its sturdy plant stays a relatively modest 3.5 feet tall. It is a late bloomer, often not opening its enormous flowers until late summer or early fall, but the scale and purity of color make the wait worthwhile for show growers and garden display alike. Because the plant's thick stems must support an unusually heavy bloom on a comparatively short frame, stake firmly and feed well through the growing season.

common_name: Bluetiful Dahlia (Blue-Lavender Periwinkle Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost; a compact, sturdy plant that needs only modest staking for its size.

directions: Bluetiful earns its name by coming about as close to true blue as a dahlia gets, with ruffled 6-inch blooms in a blue-lavender that reads almost periwinkle depending on the light. The plant is compact and sturdy at about 3.5 feet, holding its fancy, ruffled flowers upright without excessive staking. Its unusual color makes it a stand-out in mixed cutting beds, and consistent deadheading keeps the show going from midsummer through the first fall frosts.

common_name: Golden Rain Chrysanthemum (Yellow Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Golden Rain is a spider-type exhibition mum grown to NCS Class 11 standards.

directions: Golden Rain is a spider-form chrysanthemum whose narrow, drooping yellow ray florets curl tightly at their tips, giving the whole bloom the look of a shower of curly golden threads falling from the center. Grown as a single disbudded stem, pinch once in late spring to set the terminal bud and remove all competing side buds so the plant channels its energy into one large exhibition flower. It is a late-season bloomer that benefits from a frost-free finish under cover in cooler climates, and stock should be propagated fresh from basal cuttings each year rather than carried over from an aging clump.

common_name: Vienna Waltz Chrysanthemum (Pink Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; this large-flowered pink spider type is disbudded for exhibition size.

directions: Vienna Waltz produces large, fully double pink blooms built from fine, tubular spider florets that radiate outward and curl gently at their tips. As with other exhibition spiders, pinch the plant once to set a single terminal bud, strip all side buds along the stem, and stake early since the finished flower head is large relative to the stem. Propagate new stock from basal cuttings taken off the parent clump each spring, and overwinter stock plants under cover in regions with hard winters.

common_name: Senkyo Kenshin Chrysanthemum (Peach-and-Terracotta Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; a popular spider type with both specialty cut-flower growers and exhibitors.

directions: Senkyo Kenshin blends warm peach and terracotta tones through its fine, thread-like florets, with a noticeably lighter apricot shade showing on the reverse of each petal, a bicolor effect that becomes more visible as the bloom opens fully. It shares the same disbudding culture as other spiders, pinched once to set a single terminal flower with all side buds removed, and benefits from staking as the flower develops. Its warm coloring and fine texture have made it popular with cut-flower farms as well as traditional chrysanthemum exhibitors.

common_name: Pink Splendor Chrysanthemum (Pink Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; classed as a Size A pink spider type in NCS show schedules.

directions: Pink Splendor carries long, finely coiled pink florets typical of the spider division, building into a full, airy bloom with real presence on the show bench. Grow it as a single disbudded stem, pinching once to set the terminal bud and removing side buds as they appear so all the plant's energy goes into the one flower. Stake early since the developing bloom is heavy relative to the stem, and finish plants under cover where autumn frosts arrive before the bloom matures.

common_name: Alabama Chrysanthemum (Red Spoon-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; an NCS Class 9 spoon-type exhibition mum grown as a disbudded single stem.

directions: Alabama is a red spoon-form chrysanthemum whose tubular ray florets flare open at the very tip into small, rounded spoon shapes, letting glimpses of the central disc show through between the petals rather than hiding it completely as a quill does. Pinch the plant once in late spring to set a single terminal bud, remove all side buds, and stake early to support the finished flower. Like other exhibition classes, propagate fresh stock from basal cuttings each year and protect developing buds from heavy rain, which can damage the delicate spoon tips.

common_name: Buff Rayonnante Chrysanthemum (Buff-Bronze Quill-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; a midseason quill type that blooms reliably in mid-October in most of the US.

directions: Buff Rayonnante bears straight, tubular florets in a warm buff-bronze tone, radiating evenly outward around a hidden center in the classic quill arrangement where every ray stays closed to its tip rather than flaring open. As a midseason bloomer, it reaches finished bloom around mid-October in most temperate gardens, making timing of the final disbud less critical than for later exhibition classes. Pinch once to set the terminal bud, remove side buds promptly, and stake the stem as the quill head fills out and adds weight.

common_name: Atomic Chrysanthemum (Bronze-and-Yellow Quill-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; a large bicolor quill type grown as a disbudded single stem for exhibition.

directions: Atomic produces a large, bold bloom combining bronze and yellow in the same flower, its straight tubular quill florets staying closed to the tip in the typical quill manner while the bicolor shading gives the finished head real depth. Pinch once to set the single terminal bud, remove all side buds promptly, and stake early since the large bicolor flower is heavy once fully developed. Propagate from basal cuttings each year for the strongest show-quality stems.

common_name: Anzac Chrysanthemum (Bronze Anemone-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; an NCS Class 8 anemone-type exhibition mum.

directions: Anzac carries the typical anemone form, with a raised cushion of tubular bronze disc florets rising from the center while a single flat ring of outer ray florets lies around the base, giving the bloom a two-tiered look distinct from a plain single flower. Grow it as a single disbudded stem, pinching once to set the terminal bud and removing every competing side bud so the plant's energy goes entirely into that one cushioned flower. Stake early and protect the raised center from heavy rain, which can flatten and discolor the disc florets before the show.

common_name: Mancetta Sunset Chrysanthemum (Bronze Anemone-Type Mum with Golden Center)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; a reliable October-blooming anemone type popular with cut-flower growers.

directions: Mancetta Sunset forms 3-inch anemone blooms with a ring of warm bronze outer ray florets surrounding a large, raised golden-yellow cushion center, a sunset-toned combination that gives the cultivar its name. It is a dependable October bloomer that can be grown as a spray with multiple flowers per stem or disbudded to one larger bloom per stem for exhibition. Its sturdy stems and long vase life make it as useful for cutting gardens as for the show bench.

common_name: Lily Anderton Chrysanthemum (Heirloom Pink-to-Melon Anemone Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; an heirloom anemone type in the Anderton family of garden mums, blooming mid-to-late season.

directions: Lily Anderton is an heirloom anemone-form mum whose 2.5-inch daisy-like blooms open a soft pink and gradually mature into a deeper melon-pink, a color shift that gives a single planting two distinct looks over its bloom period. Reaching about 4 feet, it is related to but distinct from the similarly heirloom Harry Anderton, with its own softer, warmer color range. Its daisy-like form works as a substitute for true daisies in fall arrangements, and it blooms reliably from mid to late season with minimal disbudding required.

common_name: Yoko Ono Chrysanthemum (Bright Spring-Green Pompon Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; valued by specialty cut-flower growers for its rare green color.

directions: Yoko Ono is a small, fully double pompon mum in an unusual bright spring-green shade rarely seen in chrysanthemums, making it a sought-after novelty for designers who want true green tones without dyeing flowers. It can be grown as a spray type, left to produce many smallish blooms per stem, or lightly disbudded for a somewhat larger flower count per stem. The color stays truest when plants are grown in full sun with even moisture and harvested as blooms fully open.
